summary.text: Let \(L_0=4,L_1=16,L_2=63\) and \(L_{n+3}=4L_{n+2}-L_n\); the discrepancy \(D_n=L_{n+1}^2-L_{n+2}L_n\) satisfies a positive linear recurrence, and induction using the growth of \(L_n\) gives \(0<D_n\le L_n\). Hence \(\lceil L_{n+1}^2/L_n\rceil-1=L_{n+2}\), so induction identifies the original nonlinear sequence with \(L\), yielding the claimed linear recurrence and generating function.

full_proof.text:
Let \((b_n)_{n\ge 0}\) be the sequence given by the original definition. Thus
\[
b_0=4,\qquad b_1=16,
\]
and, for every \(n\ge 0\), \(b_{n+2}\) is the greatest integer for which
\[
\frac{b_{n+2}}{b_{n+1}}<\frac{b_{n+1}}{b_n}.
\]
Whenever \(b_n,b_{n+1}>0\), this inequality is equivalent to
\[
b_{n+2}<\frac{b_{n+1}^2}{b_n}.
\]
For any real number \(x\), the greatest integer strictly less than \(x\) is \(\lceil x\rceil-1\), including when \(x\) itself is an integer. Consequently the original rule can be written as
\[
b_{n+2}=\left\lceil\frac{b_{n+1}^2}{b_n}\right\rceil-1. \tag{1}
\]
We will prove that this nonlinear ceiling recurrence produces the integer sequence satisfying
\[
b_0=4,\quad b_1=16,\quad b_2=63,
\qquad b_n=4b_{n-1}-b_{n-3}\quad(n\ge3). \tag{2}
\]
The claimed generating function will then follow immediately.

Define an auxiliary integer sequence \((L_n)_{n\ge0}\) by
\[
L_0=4,\qquad L_1=16,\qquad L_2=63,
\]
and
\[
L_{n+3}=4L_{n+2}-L_n\qquad(n\ge0). \tag{3}
\]
Its first few terms are
\[
4,16,63,248,976,3841,\ldots.
\]
The main task is to prove that this linear-recurrence sequence also obeys the ceiling recurrence (1). For that purpose, define a second integer sequence \((D_n)_{n\ge0}\) by
\[
D_0=4,\qquad D_1=1,\qquad D_2=16,
\]
and
\[
D_{n+3}=4D_{n+1}+D_n\qquad(n\ge0). \tag{4}
\]
We will establish the identity
\[
L_{n+1}^2-L_{n+2}L_n=D_n \qquad(n\ge0), \tag{5}
\]
together with the crucial bounds
\[
1\le D_n\le L_n. \tag{6}
\]
These bounds say that \(L_{n+1}^2\) lies strictly above \(L_{n+2}L_n\), but by no more than one full multiple of \(L_n\). That is exactly what is needed to control the ceiling in (1).

We first record positivity and growth properties of \(L_n\). We claim that for every \(n\ge0\),
\[
L_n>0\qquad\text{and}\qquad L_{n+1}\ge3L_n. \tag{7}
\]
For \(n=0\), this is \(4>0\) and \(16\ge3\cdot4\). For \(n=1\), it is \(16>0\) and \(63\ge3\cdot16\). Now suppose the assertions have been established through the indices needed below. In particular, suppose
\[
L_{n+1}>0,
\qquad L_{n+2}\ge3L_{n+1},
\qquad L_{n+1}\ge3L_n,
\qquad L_n>0.
\]
Then \(L_{n+2}>0\). Moreover, by (3),
\[
L_{n+3}=4L_{n+2}-L_n.
\]
Since the preceding growth inequalities imply \(L_{n+2}\ge L_n\), we get
\[
L_{n+3}=3L_{n+2}+(L_{n+2}-L_n)\ge3L_{n+2}.
\]
This proves (7) by strong induction. In particular every \(L_n\) is a positive integer, so all the quotients used later have positive denominators.

We next prove (5). Let
\[
E_n:=L_{n+1}^2-L_{n+2}L_n.
\]
Direct calculation gives the first three values. From (3),
\[
L_3=4L_2-L_0=4\cdot63-4=248,
\]
and
\[
L_4=4L_3-L_1=4\cdot248-16=976.
\]
Therefore
\[
E_0=16^2-63\cdot4=256-252=4,
\]
\[
E_1=63^2-248\cdot16=3969-3968=1,
\]
and
\[
E_2=248^2-976\cdot63=61504-61488=16.
\]
Thus \(E_0,E_1,E_2\) agree with \(D_0,D_1,D_2\).

It remains to see that \(E_n\) satisfies the same recurrence as \(D_n\). Write
\[
a=L_n,\qquad b=L_{n+1},\qquad c=L_{n+2}.
\]
Repeated use of (3) gives
\[
L_{n+3}=4c-a,
\]
\[
L_{n+4}=4(4c-a)-b=16c-4a-b,
\]
and
\[
L_{n+5}=4(16c-4a-b)-c=63c-16a-4b.
\]
Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
E_{n+3}
&=L_{n+4}^2-L_{n+5}L_{n+3}\\
&=(16c-4a-b)^2-(63c-16a-4b)(4c-a)\\
&=4ab-ac+b^2-16bc+4c^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
On the other hand,
\[
E_n=b^2-ac
\]
and
\[
E_{n+1}=c^2-L_{n+3}b=c^2-(4c-a)b=c^2-4bc+ab.
\]
It follows that
\[
4E_{n+1}+E_n
=4c^2-16bc+4ab+b^2-ac
=E_{n+3}.
\]
Thus
\[
E_{n+3}=4E_{n+1}+E_n,
\]
which is precisely recurrence (4). Since the first three values agree, induction proves \(E_n=D_n\) for every \(n\), establishing (5).

The lower bound in (6) follows from positivity of \(D_n\). Indeed, \(D_0=4\), \(D_1=1\), and \(D_2=16\) are positive. If the earlier terms are positive, then recurrence (4) gives
\[
D_{n+3}=4D_{n+1}+D_n>0.
\]
Therefore \(D_n\) is a positive integer for every \(n\), so \(D_n\ge1\).

We now prove the upper bound \(D_n\le L_n\) by strong induction. It holds initially because
\[
D_0=4=L_0,
\qquad D_1=1\le16=L_1,
\qquad D_2=16\le63=L_2.
\]
Suppose that \(D_{n+1}\le L_{n+1}\) and \(D_n\le L_n\). Then
\[
D_{n+3}=4D_{n+1}+D_n
\le4L_{n+1}+L_n. \tag{8}
\]
We compare this with
\[
L_{n+3}=4L_{n+2}-L_n. \tag{9}
\]
The growth estimate (7) implies both \(L_n\le L_{n+1}\) and \(L_{n+2}\ge3L_{n+1}\). Consequently
\[
4L_{n+1}+2L_n
\le6L_{n+1}
\le12L_{n+1}
\le4L_{n+2}.
\]
In particular,
\[
4L_{n+1}+L_n\le4L_{n+2}-L_n=L_{n+3}.
\]
Together with (8), this gives \(D_{n+3}\le L_{n+3}\), completing the induction. We have therefore proved the full bound
\[
1\le D_n\le L_n
\]
for every \(n\).

We can now show that \(L_n\) satisfies the nonlinear original recurrence. Identity (5) can be rearranged as
\[
L_{n+1}^2=L_{n+2}L_n+D_n. \tag{10}
\]
Divide by the positive integer \(L_n\):
\[
\frac{L_{n+1}^2}{L_n}=L_{n+2}+\frac{D_n}{L_n}. \tag{11}
\]
Because \(1\le D_n\le L_n\), we have
\[
0<\frac{D_n}{L_n}\le1.
\]
Thus the ceiling of the right side of (11) is exactly \(L_{n+2}+1\), whether \(D_n<L_n\) or \(D_n=L_n\). Therefore
\[
\left\lceil\frac{L_{n+1}^2}{L_n}\right\rceil-1=L_{n+2}. \tag{12}
\]
This is exactly recurrence (1).

For completeness, the same conclusion can be expressed entirely in terms of integer division. Since for positive \(q\),
\[
\left\lceil\frac{p}{q}\right\rceil
=\left\lfloor\frac{p+q-1}{q}\right\rfloor,
\]
substituting (10) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\left\lfloor\frac{L_{n+1}^2+L_n-1}{L_n}\right\rfloor
&=\left\lfloor\frac{L_{n+2}L_n+D_n+L_n-1}{L_n}\right\rfloor\\
&=L_{n+2}+
\left\lfloor\frac{D_n+L_n-1}{L_n}\right\rfloor.
\end{aligned}
\]
The inequalities \(1\le D_n\le L_n\) imply
\[
L_n\le D_n+L_n-1<2L_n,
\]
so the last floor is \(1\). Subtracting \(1\) again yields \(L_{n+2}\).

It remains to identify the sequence from the original definition with \(L_n\). We do this by strong induction. The initial values agree:
\[
b_0=4=L_0,
\qquad b_1=16=L_1.
\]
Assume that \(b_n=L_n\) and \(b_{n+1}=L_{n+1}\). In particular these terms are positive by (7), so the original extremal rule is equivalent to the ceiling formula (1). Using the induction hypothesis and then (12),
\[
\begin{aligned}
b_{n+2}
&=\left\lceil\frac{b_{n+1}^2}{b_n}\right\rceil-1\\
&=\left\lceil\frac{L_{n+1}^2}{L_n}\right\rceil-1\\
&=L_{n+2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(b_n=L_n\) for all \(n\ge0\). In particular \(b_2=L_2=63\), and recurrence (3) gives
\[
b_{n+3}=4b_{n+2}-b_n\qquad(n\ge0),
\]
or equivalently
\[
b_n=4b_{n-1}-b_{n-3}\qquad(n\ge3).
\]
The positivity and growth already proved ensure that the subtraction here gives a positive integer.

Finally, let
\[
G(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}b_nx^n
\]
be the ordinary generating function, regarded as a formal power series. Multiplying the recurrence by \(x^n\) and summing over \(n\ge3\) gives
\[
\sum_{n\ge3}b_nx^n
=4\sum_{n\ge3}b_{n-1}x^n
-\sum_{n\ge3}b_{n-3}x^n.
\]
In terms of \(G(x)\), this is
\[
G(x)-b_0-b_1x-b_2x^2
=4x\bigl(G(x)-b_0-b_1x\bigr)-x^3G(x).
\]
Therefore
\[
(1-4x+x^3)G(x)
=b_0+(b_1-4b_0)x+(b_2-4b_1)x^2.
\]
Substituting \(b_0=4\), \(b_1=16\), and \(b_2=63\), the right side becomes
\[
4+(16-64)x+(63-64)x^2=4-x^2.
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{G(x)=\frac{4-x^2}{1-4x+x^3}}.
\]
Thus the sequence produced by the original greatest-integer consecutive-ratio rule is exactly the sequence with the conjectured generating function.
